briefs.problem: Technician routes are built and rebuilt with no defined logic for handling late-notice cancellations, causing wasted travel time and ad hoc, inconsistent replanning.
briefs.solution: A maintenance-visit scheduling system that builds technician tours and reacts to late cancellations by replanning the affected tour.
introduces: a tour/route construction engine assigning visits to technicians
a planner/dispatcher administrative surface not previously named
real-time synchronization with a technician-facing mobile app
concurrency handling across simultaneous cancellations and technician availability changes

challenges.headline: Gap-fill vs. simple reshuffle
challenges.premise: The request assumes a 'replanification' capability without saying whether a cancelled slot should be offered to another waiting client or simply absorbed into the technician's remaining stops.
challenges.alternative: A first version that just reorders the technician's remaining tour around the gap is far smaller than a waitlist-matching dispatch engine, and can ship while the waitlist need is validated separately.
challenges.consequence: Building a full backfill/dispatch engine for a need that was never confirmed multiplies the system's complexity, timeline and cost for a capability the client may not actually want.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client which behavior they expect from a cancellation before estimating or architecting anything.

challenges.headline: Unsupervised automatic replanning
challenges.premise: The request implies the system replans the tour on its own after a cancellation, but no planner or approval step is described.
challenges.alternative: Routing a proposed replan through a planner for validation before it reaches the technician avoids exposing customers and technicians to unreviewed automated changes, at the cost of one extra step.
challenges.consequence: Fully automated replanning with no human check can misfire (wrong slot, technician conflict, unwanted customer contact) with no safety net, and is hard to walk back once technicians depend on it.
challenges.recommendation: Decide with the client whether replanning is automatic, planner-validated, or hybrid before building the workflow.

challenges.headline: Recurring-contract visit assumption
challenges.premise: Visits are assumed to originate from recurring maintenance contracts, but this is only a working hypothesis.
challenges.alternative: If visits are actually created on demand, tour generation becomes a real-time slot-allocation problem rather than a periodic-schedule optimization — a materially different engine.
challenges.consequence: Designing the scheduling core around a fixed recurring model, if visits are actually ad hoc, would force a rebuild of the tour-generation logic later.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm the source and cadence of maintenance visits before choosing the scheduling architecture.

complexity_reasons: dynamic re-routing logic whose exact behavior (reshuffle vs backfill) is still undefined
concurrency across simultaneous cancellations and technician availability
real-time mobile sync and notification requirements
no confirmed assignment rules or visit-origin model to build the core on
briefs.cost_driver: the cancellation-handling engine — whichever of reshuffle or waitlist-backfill it turns out to be
risks: Committing to a waitlist/dispatch architecture before confirming the client actually needs it, causing costly rework
No documented current process, making it hard to size effort or set realistic user expectations
Undefined technician-client assignment rules — if they vary by zone, skill or contract, tour-building logic may need significant rework once discovered
No permission model defined, risking unsupervised automated changes reaching customers or technicians
No success metrics agreed, making it hard to know what 'optimized' actually means for this client

opportunities.text: Build the tour-construction logic as a distinct, reusable optimization component, separate from the cancellation-handling rules, so the two can evolve independently.
Generalize the cancellation notification path into an event-driven notification framework that could later cover other trigger types (delays, reassignments).

next_steps: Run a short scoping session to settle the cancellation-handling model (reshuffle vs waitlist backfill) and the technician-client assignment rules — these two decisions shape the entire architecture.
Document today's scheduling process and agree on 2-3 success metrics, to baseline effort and define what 'better' means for this client.
Confirm whether a planner/dispatcher role exists and whether replanning should be automatic or validated, before any workflow or permission design starts.

decisions.decision: Core entities are Client, Maintenance Visit, Technician, and Tour
A planner/dispatcher role is assumed necessary alongside technicians and clients
decisions.why: Someone needs to own tour construction and likely validate automated replanning decisions.
decisions.alternative: Fully automated rescheduling with no dedicated human role.
decisions.tradeoff: An extra role and workflow step, in exchange for a safety net on customer-facing schedule changes.

Acceptance criteria and rollout plan

briefs.problem: Technician tours are planned with no defined rule for who gets assigned where, and late client cancellations leave a freed slot with no agreed mechanism for what happens to it.
briefs.solution: A tool to build technician maintenance tours and handle late-cancellation rescheduling, automatically or with planner assistance.
introduces: a rescheduling/reallocation mechanism for freed slots
an assignment-rule engine binding visits to technicians and tours
a notification layer for technicians and clients on schedule changes
concurrency handling for simultaneous cancellations across tours
a planner/dispatcher administration surface, if that role is confirmed

challenges.headline: Automatic slot-refill assumed
challenges.premise: The request treats 'replanification' as if the mechanism is obvious, without saying whether a freed slot is auto-filled, left empty, or manually reassigned.
challenges.alternative: Start with a freed slot surfaced to a planner for manual reassignment, and only build automatic waitlist-matching once assignment rules are proven stable — this avoids committing to a matching engine before the rules it depends on exist.
challenges.consequence: Building an automated refill mechanism before the assignment rule is defined risks engineering the wrong engine, or a far more complex one than the client actually needs.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether they expect a simple assisted calendar or a fully automated rescheduling engine before scoping or estimating.

challenges.headline: Efficiency problem unverified
challenges.premise: The stated objective — reducing manual planning effort and disorganization from late cancellations — is an inference, not something the client has confirmed or measured.
challenges.alternative: Capture the current process (Excel, paper, another tool) and a concrete success measure (fewer kilometers, fewer missed visits, faster replanning) before committing to a build.
challenges.consequence: Without a baseline or a defined 'better', the team risks over-building a sophisticated scheduling engine to solve a problem a shared calendar could fix.
challenges.recommendation: Run a short discovery session on current process and success metrics before scoping the build.

challenges.headline: Assignment logic left undefined
challenges.premise: The request assumes visits get slotted into technician tours, without saying whether that's by zone, skill, assigned client, or plain availability.
challenges.alternative: Nail down the actual assignment criterion with operations before building anything — zone-based routing and skill-matching are structurally different engines, not variants of the same one.
challenges.consequence: Guessing this after the build starts risks rebuilding the core scheduling logic once the real rule surfaces.
challenges.recommendation: Workshop the assignment rule (zone/skill/client/availability) with the ops team before any engineering begins.

complexity_reasons: core rescheduling mechanism undefined (auto-refill vs manual)
assignment rule to technician/tour unknown (zone, skill, client)
technician constraints (availability, geography, visit duration) not captured
no success metric to bound scope between a calendar and an optimization engine
briefs.cost_driver: the rescheduling/reallocation logic for freed slots after a late cancellation
risks: Committing to an automated slot-filling engine before assignment rules are confirmed could force a rebuild of the core logic.
No visibility into the current process means migration effort and existing data reuse are unestimated.
Permissions (who can edit a tour, validate a reschedule) are undefined and typically surface late, during acceptance testing.
Multiple late cancellations processed the same day, across tours, could create reassignment conflicts if any automation is introduced without a defined resolution rule.

opportunities.text: Generalize the cancellation-to-reschedule flow into a reusable reallocation engine once assignment rules stabilize.
Build a single notification hook for schedule changes (cancellation, reassignment) reusable by both technician and client-facing views.

next_steps: Run a discovery session to capture the current planning process and a concrete success metric before scoping anything.
Workshop the assignment rule (zone, skill, assigned client, or availability) and the exact rescheduling mechanism (auto-refill vs manual) with operations.
Confirm actors and permissions: who creates a visit, who owns a tour, who is allowed to reschedule or validate a change.

decisions.decision: The core objects are Visit, Client, Technician and Tour, with the technician executing the tour and the client as the visit recipient who can cancel.

exclusions.option: A multi-client, configurable rule-management layer (per-client assignment or escalation rules)
exclusions.reason: Nothing in the request suggests multiple client organizations sharing the tool — it reads as an internal tool for a single structure, so building configurability for multi-tenancy now is unwarranted.

exclusions.option: A fully automated geo/skill-based route-optimization engine
exclusions.reason: The assignment rule and technician constraints (zone, skills, availability) are not yet defined, so committing engineering effort to an optimization algorithm now would be built on guesses.

open_decisions: What happens to a freed slot after a late cancellation: left empty, auto-filled from a waitlist, or manually reassigned — and what counts as 'late'?
The rule for assigning a visit to a technician/tour: zone, skill, assigned client, or availability, and whether it varies by client or intervention type.
Who creates, owns, and can modify a tour: a planner, the technician, or an automated process.
The current planning process (tool, format) and whether existing data needs migration.
Technician-side constraints: working hours, geographic coverage, average visit duration, required skills.
The measure of success: fewer kilometers, fewer missed visits, faster replanning, or something else.

briefs.solution: A planning tool that organizes maintenance visits into per-technician tours and handles rescheduling when a client cancels late.

challenges.headline: Manual tool vs optimization engine
challenges.premise: The request assumes a technician-tour planning tool without saying whether routes must be computed/optimized automatically.
challenges.alternative: Start with a manual/assisted tool where a dispatcher assigns and reorders visits by hand, and add automatic route optimization later once volume justifies the investment.
challenges.consequence: Building a route-optimization engine when a simple visual planner was actually wanted multiplies cost and timeline by an order of magnitude for no measured benefit.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether 'tournée' means a visualized/adjustable schedule or an algorithmically optimized itinerary before estimating anything.

challenges.headline: Last-minute cancellation undefined
challenges.premise: The request treats a late cancellation as a single known trigger for 'replanification' without defining the cutoff or what happens to the freed slot.
challenges.alternative: Define an explicit lateness threshold and pick one concrete mechanism (waitlist fill-in, shortened tour, or inserted urgent visit) — each implies a different data model, not a parameter tweak.
challenges.consequence: Leaving this open risks a fragile, ad hoc rebuild once real patterns appear (several cancellations the same day, a technician unavailable, a client waiting for an earlier slot).
challenges.recommendation: Nail down the cancellation cutoff and the exact reschedule mechanism with the client before building the workflow.

challenges.headline: Visit origin left unconfirmed
challenges.premise: The request implies visits already exist and just need to be organized into tours, without saying if they come from a recurring maintenance contract or are created ad hoc.
challenges.alternative: If a contract drives a recurring frequency per client, the system needs a separate visit-generation layer distinct from tour assignment — two engines, not one.
challenges.consequence: Assuming ad hoc creation when contracts actually exist means retrofitting a recurring-generation layer later, which touches the core object model, not just a screen.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm visit origin with the client early, since it changes the object model itself.

complexity_reasons: unresolved fork between a manual planning tool and an automated route-optimization engine
rescheduling mechanism (waitlist, shortened tour, or inserted visit) undefined and each implies a different data model
concurrency risk when multiple cancellations or reassignments touch the same technician's tour
permission model and current process entirely unknown, blocking a realistic estimate
briefs.cost_driver: whether routes must be computed automatically (itinerary optimization) or organized manually by a dispatcher
risks: Building a route-optimization engine that isn't actually needed, ballooning cost and delaying delivery
Committing to a reschedule mechanism (e.g. simple shortening) that later needs a waitlist/queue model, forcing a data-model rework
Permissions being treated as an afterthought and only surfacing at acceptance testing, once the reschedule screen already exists
No visibility into the current process risks rebuilding a step that already works, or missing the client's actual pain point
Concurrent edits to the same technician's tour (dispatcher reassigning while the technician is mid-route) causing conflicting states

opportunities.text: Build the rescheduling/freed-slot logic as a capability distinct from tour assignment, so the mechanism (waitlist, reinsertion, shortening) can evolve without redesigning the core tour model.
If visit origin is confirmed as recurring maintenance contracts, keep a separate visit-generation layer from tour assignment, so changes to contract frequency don't ripple into how tours are built.
Centralize technician/client notifications (cancellation, reassignment) as a single event-driven service reusable for future schedule events.

next_steps: Run a short discovery session to capture the current process and success metrics, so the build doesn't replace something that already works and has a measurable target.
Resolve the manual-vs-optimization fork with the client before estimating — it is the single largest cost swing in the project.
Specify the cancellation threshold and the exact rescheduling mechanism, since it's the second core behavior explicitly requested and shapes the data model.
Confirm visit origin (recurring contract vs ad hoc) and define the planner/dispatcher role and permissions before designing the reschedule screen.

decisions.decision: The core object model centers on Visit, Client, Technician, and Tour
One tour is built per technician
Rescheduling after a cancellation is handled inside the system rather than left as a manual side process
decisions.why: The request explicitly names replanification as required behavior, not just cancellation tracking.
decisions.alternative: Log cancellations passively and let a dispatcher handle the actual rescheduling outside the tool.
decisions.tradeoff: In-system rescheduling adds workflow complexity now, in exchange for delivering the behavior actually requested.
